plan.contextChunk: This figure is a perspective line drawing of a rectangular coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field. The coil appears as a tall rectangular loop of several stacked turns, rendered as a striped gray band so the windings show, and tilted so its face is seen obliquely. A vertical axis labeled z passes through the coil's center, solid above and below the loop and dashed where it crosses the interior; a small circular arrow curls around its top to give the sense of rotation. A second axis labeled x runs diagonally toward the lower left, with a dashed segment continuing to the upper right. From the center point, a bold blue arrow labeled B points horizontally to the right as the uniform field, while an orange arrow labeled n-hat, the unit normal to the coil's surface, springs from the same origin and tilts down and to the right; a thin arc between the two marks the angle theta. Anchoring n-hat and B at a shared origin makes the angle between them the one quantity the reader tracks as the loop turns. The arrangement sets up the flux through a rotating coil and the emf that rotation induces.

interactions.label: Coil angle θ
interactions.teaches: The magnetic flux depends only on the component of the magnetic field through the coil area, so it follows Φ = BA cos θ as the coil normal sweeps away from B

interactions.label: Play steady rotation
interactions.teaches: A steadily rotating coil makes θ change continuously, so the flux oscillates and the induced emf appears because the flux is changing with time

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Connects the geometric angle between n-hat and B to the sinusoidal flux and emf curves used in the calculation

demo_steps.title: Oblique coil with partial flux
demo_steps.narration: The coil face is vertical and its orange normal makes an acute angle with the blue magnetic field. The flux readout shows Φ = BA cos θ, so only the field component parallel to n-hat contributes.

demo_steps.title: Maximum flux
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 0°, the coil normal is aligned with B. The field passes straight through the area vector direction, so the flux reaches its positive maximum BA.

demo_steps.title: Zero flux
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 90°, the coil normal is perpendicular to B. The magnetic field lies in the plane of the coil, so no field component passes through the area.

demo_steps.title: Same motion as waves
demo_steps.narration: In graph view, the same angle controls a cosine flux curve and a sine emf curve. The emf is largest where the flux curve is changing fastest.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a physics coordinate frame with z vertical through the coil center. Put the origin at the shared tail of B and n-hat. The rectangular coil is about 2.1 world units wide and 3.2 world units tall, centered at the origin, with its long sides vertical and its plane always containing the z-axis. At θ = 45° the coil should visually resemble the source: a tall gray rectangle seen obliquely, with its right edge slightly behind the front edge and its normal projecting down-right on screen. Draw 5 or 6 closely spaced rectangular windings, each as a gray line loop; use offsets of about 0.04 world units along the coil normal and/or slight size offsets so the left, right, top, and bottom edges appear as striped parallel gray bands. The z-axis spans roughly z = -2.2 to +2.5, black #111111, solid outside the coil and dashed where it passes through the interior; label z just above the arrowhead. The rotation arrow is a small black circular arrow of radius about 0.35 centered above the coil near z = +2.15. The x-axis lies in the horizontal plane and projects diagonally from the origin toward the lower-left of the screen; draw a black arrow from the origin to about 2.4 units in that direction and label x at the arrowhead, with a dashed continuation from the origin toward the upper-right. Include the short left horizontal reference axis seen in the source, solid farther left and dashed near the origin. The magnetic field vector B is a thick blue arrow #008fc5 from the origin to the right, length about 1.9 units, labeled B near the arrowhead. The normal vector n-hat is a thick orange arrow #f28c28 from the origin, length about 1.15 units, lying in the horizontal rotation plane; at the default θ = 45° it projects down-right relative to B. Draw the θ arc as a thin black arc of radius about 0.42 between B and n-hat, with θ label just outside the arc. Use formulas Φ = BA cos θ and ε = -dΦ/dt = BAω sin θ when θ = ωt; if displaying N turns, use flux linkage NΦ and emf NBAω sin θ, but keep the main source-style flux readout as BA cos θ. Graph view should use θ from 0 to 360 degrees along the horizontal axis; plot flux as a blue cosine curve and emf as an orange sine curve, with matched amplitude scaling for readability.
interactionPlan.notes: Implement the coil as grouped line segments that rotate about the z-axis when thetaAngle changes or steadyRotation plays. Keep B fixed in world space and rotate only the coil plus n-hat vector. The vector view should preserve the source composition: coil dominates the center-left, B points to the right, n-hat points down-right at the default angle, and axes remain thin black reference geometry. For graph view, either fade the 3D coil back and overlay the curves or switch to a clean 2D plot; the toggle should keep theta synchronized so the cursor and curve markers match the current vector angle. During animation, advance thetaAngle at constant angular speed and update coil orientation, n-hat direction, flux readout, graph cursor, flux marker, and emf marker every frame.

authoredContext:
A Rectangular Coil Rotating in a Magnetic Field A rectangular coil of area A and N turns is placed in a uniform magnetic field B→=Bj^, as shown in the figure. The coil is rotated about the z-axis through its center at a constant angular velocity ω. Obtain an expression for the induced emf in the coil.

A rectangular coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field.

Figure shows a rectangular coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field.

Strategy According to the diagram, the angle between the perpendicular to the surface (n^) and the magnetic field (B→) is θ. The dot product of B→·n^ simplifies to only the cosθ component of the magnetic field, namely where the magnetic field projects onto the unit area vector n^. The magnitude of the magnetic field and the area of the loop are fixed over time, which makes the integration simplify quickly. The induced emf is written out using Faraday’s law.
